days.progression: Begin with the image of God’s care. This foundation of trust will lead into tomorrow’s reading about grace.
days.reflection: Where do you need to trust God’s care today?
days.prayerPrompt: Name the place where you most need care, and ask God to guide you through it.

questions.prompt: What picture does David use for the LORD?
questions.explanation: David begins, “The LORD is my shepherd.” The whole psalm grows from this relationship of care and trust.

questions.prompt: Why does David say he will fear no evil in the valley?
questions.explanation: The reason is personal: “You are with me.” The danger is real, but David does not face it alone.

questions.prompt: What does David say will follow him?
questions.explanation: David closes with confidence in God’s goodness and mercy throughout his life.

days.progression: Yesterday’s shepherd picture becomes a word of grace: God’s love and mercy come before our good work.
days.reflection: What changes when you receive grace as a gift rather than treating today as something to prove?
days.prayerPrompt: Thank God for mercy, then ask for one opportunity to do good from a place of gratitude.

questions.prompt: What does Paul highlight about God before describing new life with Christ?
options: God’s great love and rich mercy
questions.explanation: Verses 4–5 begin with God’s love and mercy, then describe being made alive with Christ. God’s action is the starting point.

questions.prompt: How does Paul describe salvation in these verses?
options: An achievement that gives reason to boast
A reward for a flawless record
A gift of God, received through faith
questions.explanation: Paul calls salvation God’s gift and excludes boasting in works. The passage invites gratitude for grace.

questions.prompt: What purpose follows the description of believers as God’s workmanship?
options: To compare their worth with others
questions.explanation: Verse 10 says believers are created in Christ Jesus to do good works. Good action belongs in the life grace makes possible.

days.progression: After naming grace as a gift, notice how Jesus pictures welcome. The father reaches toward both of his sons.
days.reflection: Which part of this story do you need to sit with: returning, being welcomed, or making room for someone else?
days.prayerPrompt: Bring an honest confession or resentment to God, and ask for a heart that can receive and extend mercy.

questions.prompt: What does the father do when he sees his younger son still far away?
options: Waits for him to earn a place back
Sends a servant to turn him away
Runs to him and embraces him
questions.explanation: The father sees his son, is filled with compassion, runs, and embraces him. Jesus makes the father’s welcome vivid and active.

questions.prompt: How does the father respond when the older son refuses to join the celebration?
options: He comes out and pleads with him
He locks the door against him
He ignores the older son’s anger
questions.explanation: The father goes out to the older son too. His invitation reaches the son who stayed home as well as the son who returned.

questions.prompt: Why does the father say it is fitting to celebrate?
options: The brother who was lost has been found
Both brothers have earned a prize
questions.explanation: The father describes his son as dead and alive again, lost and found. The celebration centers on his return.

days.progression: The welcome in yesterday’s story becomes a direct invitation from Jesus: come, learn, and find rest.
days.reflection: What burden can you name honestly, and what might learning from Jesus look like within it?
days.prayerPrompt: Tell Jesus what has made you weary, and ask to learn His gentleness in your next small step.

questions.prompt: Whom does Jesus invite to come to Him?
options: Those who are weary and burdened
Only those who already feel strong
questions.explanation: Jesus addresses the weary and burdened. Need is the setting of the invitation, rather than a barrier to it.

questions.prompt: How does Jesus describe His own heart?
questions.explanation: Jesus says He is gentle and humble in heart as He invites people to take His yoke and learn from Him.

questions.prompt: Along with coming to Him, what does Jesus invite people to do?
options: Take His yoke and learn from Him
questions.explanation: The invitation includes learning from Jesus. Rest and discipleship appear together in His words.

days.progression: Receiving rest does not require pretending pain has vanished. Today’s lament places hope beside remembered sorrow.
days.reflection: What sorrow do you need to acknowledge, and what small sign of mercy can you notice alongside it?
days.prayerPrompt: Name what hurts without tidying it up, then ask for enough hope to meet this day.

questions.prompt: What is the speaker remembering before turning toward hope?
questions.explanation: Verses 19–20 remember affliction and a humbled soul. The hope that follows is spoken from within grief.

questions.prompt: What is described as new every morning?
questions.explanation: Verses 22–23 connect the LORD’s unfailing mercies with each new morning and praise His faithfulness.

questions.prompt: What response does this passage commend while waiting for the LORD?
options: Pretending there has been no grief
Measuring hope only by immediate results
questions.explanation: Verses 25–26 describe seeking the LORD and waiting quietly for His salvation. Hope can include patient waiting.

days.progression: Having begun with care and mercy, now hear Jesus’ call. Following starts with responding to Him where you are.
days.reflection: What familiar habit or distraction might you set down to pay attention to Jesus today?
days.prayerPrompt: Ask for willingness to respond to Jesus and courage for one clear, faithful step.

questions.prompt: What response does Jesus call for as He announces God’s kingdom?
options: Seek a more important social position
Repent and believe in the gospel
questions.explanation: Jesus announces that the time is fulfilled and God’s kingdom is near, then calls people to repent and believe the gospel.

questions.prompt: What are Simon and Andrew doing when Jesus calls them?
options: Casting a fishing net into the sea
Teaching a crowd in the synagogue
questions.explanation: Mark places Jesus’ call in the brothers’ working day. They are casting a net because they are fishermen.

questions.prompt: How do Simon and Andrew respond to the call?
options: They send someone else in their place
They leave their nets and follow Him
They ask the crowd to decide for them
questions.explanation: Verse 18 describes an immediate response: they leave their nets and follow Jesus. The focus is their response to His invitation.

days.progression: Yesterday’s first response grows into an ongoing relationship. Jesus describes following as remaining in Him and learning His love.
days.reflection: What would remaining close to Jesus look like in one ordinary part of your day?
days.prayerPrompt: Ask Jesus to help you remain close to Him and make His love visible in one relationship today.

questions.prompt: In Jesus’ picture, who is the true vine?
questions.explanation: Jesus identifies Himself as the true vine and His Father as the keeper of the vineyard.

questions.prompt: What does Jesus ask His disciples to do?
questions.explanation: The branch bears fruit through its connection to the vine. Jesus calls His disciples to remain in Him.

questions.prompt: What command does Jesus give about love?
options: Love one another as He has loved them
questions.explanation: Jesus makes His own love the pattern for the disciples’ love for one another.

days.progression: Remaining close takes attention. Notice Mary’s listening and Martha’s worry, and make room to hear before you act.
days.reflection: Where could you make a little room to listen without turning that space into another performance?
days.prayerPrompt: Bring your distractions to Jesus and ask for an attentive, unhurried heart.

questions.prompt: Who welcomes Jesus into her home?
questions.explanation: Luke begins this scene with Martha welcoming Jesus. Her hospitality is part of the setting for the conversation.

questions.prompt: What does Mary do at the Lord’s feet?
questions.explanation: Verse 39 specifically describes Mary listening to the Lord’s message. Attention to His words is the center of her action.

questions.prompt: What does Jesus name when He speaks to Martha?
options: Her worry and upset about many things
A refusal to welcome any guests
A lack of ability to prepare food
questions.explanation: Jesus addresses Martha’s worry and agitation, then affirms Mary’s choice. The passage does not say hospitality itself is wrong.

days.progression: Listening leads to action shaped by Jesus. Watch Him use His authority to serve the people at His table.
days.reflection: What ordinary act of service could you offer without needing recognition?
days.prayerPrompt: Thank Jesus for His example and ask for the humility to serve someone in a practical way.

questions.prompt: What practical action does Jesus take during the meal?
questions.explanation: Jesus takes a towel, pours water into a basin, and washes the disciples’ feet. The scene makes His service concrete.

questions.prompt: Which titles does Jesus affirm before explaining His example?
questions.explanation: Jesus affirms that He is their Teacher and Lord. His place of authority gives weight to the example of serving.

questions.prompt: What does Jesus want His disciples to do with His example?
options: Do as He has done for them
Reserve service for people of higher rank
questions.explanation: Jesus says He has given an example for His disciples to follow. Verse 17 connects knowing these things with doing them.

days.progression: The call to follow, remain, listen, and serve comes together here: Jesus asks hearers to practice His words.
days.reflection: Which teaching from these first ten days can become one concrete action today?
days.prayerPrompt: Ask for help to turn one thing you have heard into something you actually do.

questions.prompt: Who is compared to the wise builder?
options: Someone who hears Jesus’ words and acts on them
Someone who hears but never acts
Someone who avoids hearing difficult words
questions.explanation: Jesus joins hearing and doing in the picture of the wise builder. The foundation is a practiced response to His teaching.

questions.prompt: What happens to the house built on the rock when the storm comes?
options: It never encounters wind or rain
It is moved to a different hillside
questions.explanation: The storm reaches the house, but it does not fall because its foundation is on rock. The story does not promise a storm-free life.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes the foolish builder from the wise builder?
options: Having heard a different set of words
Encountering a storm for the first time
Hearing Jesus’ words without acting on them
questions.explanation: Both pictures involve hearing and a storm. The contrast is whether the hearer acts on Jesus’ words.

days.progression: Practicing Jesus’ words includes learning to pray and trust. Begin this part of the journey with the Father’s care and His kingdom.
days.reflection: Which concern can you bring to your Father instead of carrying it alone?
days.prayerPrompt: Address God as Father, name a real need, and ask to seek His kingdom in how you meet it.

questions.prompt: How does Jesus teach His disciples to address God in prayer?
questions.explanation: Jesus begins the prayer with “Our Father in heaven,” holding together closeness and reverence.

questions.prompt: What example does Jesus use when teaching about worry over food?
questions.explanation: Jesus points to the birds, which the heavenly Father feeds, and reminds His hearers of their value.

questions.prompt: What does Jesus say to seek first?
questions.explanation: Jesus places God’s kingdom and righteousness at the center of life, within His teaching about worry and trust.

days.progression: Trust gives you room for honesty. This short psalm holds questions, a request for help, and remembered goodness together.
days.reflection: What honest question have you been reluctant to bring into prayer?
days.prayerPrompt: Tell God what feels long or unresolved, ask for help, and name any goodness you can remember.

questions.prompt: Which question is repeated in the opening of the psalm?
questions.explanation: The repeated question gives voice to felt absence, sorrow, and pressure from an enemy. The psalm makes room for distress in prayer.

questions.prompt: What does the psalmist ask God to do?
options: Pretend the danger is not real
questions.explanation: Verse 3 turns the lament into a direct request for God’s attention and help. The speaker does not hide his need.

questions.prompt: What does the psalmist say he has trusted in?
options: His own ability to control the outcome
questions.explanation: The psalmist names God’s loving devotion and salvation, then recalls God’s goodness in verse 6. Trust appears beside the earlier questions.

days.progression: After an honest lament, return to Jesus as a teacher of prayer. He invites requests for daily needs and persistent trust.
days.reflection: What simple need can you bring to God today, without feeling you must find impressive words?
days.prayerPrompt: Ask for today’s provision and forgiveness, then ask the Father for the help of His Spirit.

questions.prompt: What request begins this teaching about prayer?
options: Lord, give us places of honor
Lord, explain how to impress the crowds
questions.explanation: A disciple asks Jesus to teach them to pray after seeing Him pray. Learning prayer starts with a request for help.

questions.prompt: What everyday need is included in the prayer Jesus teaches?
options: A larger storehouse than a neighbor’s
questions.explanation: Jesus includes a request for each day’s bread. Ordinary needs have a place in prayer alongside God’s name and kingdom.

questions.prompt: What gift does Jesus say the heavenly Father will give to those who ask Him?
questions.explanation: Jesus ends this teaching by naming the Holy Spirit as the Father’s gift. That conclusion helps keep the invitation to ask centered on God’s care.

days.theme: Prayer in the middle of life
days.progression: Persistent asking can be joined with gratitude. Paul brings requests, peace, and learned contentment into the same everyday life.
days.reflection: Name one concern and one reason for gratitude. Bring both into prayer.
days.prayerPrompt: Bring God one concern and one reason for thanks, and ask for His peace as you take the next step.

questions.prompt: What does Paul say should accompany our requests to God?
questions.explanation: Paul joins prayer and petition with thanksgiving, inviting believers to bring their requests to God.

questions.prompt: What will guard hearts and minds in Christ Jesus?
questions.explanation: Paul speaks of God’s peace guarding hearts and minds, not a promise that all circumstances become easy.

questions.prompt: What has Paul learned in different circumstances?
questions.explanation: Paul describes contentment learned in both need and abundance. His words about strength in Christ belong in that setting.

days.progression: Thanksgiving grows when you remember who God is. Finish these days of prayer by noticing compassion, forgiveness, and human frailty.
days.reflection: Which expression of God’s compassion in this psalm helps you pray with gratitude today?
days.prayerPrompt: Name one kindness you do not want to forget, and thank God for compassion toward your limits.

questions.prompt: What does the psalmist urge his soul not to forget?
questions.explanation: The call to praise is joined to remembrance. Verse 2 asks the speaker’s own soul to remember the LORD’s kind deeds.

questions.prompt: How does the psalm describe the LORD’s character?
options: Quick to anger and reluctant to show kindness
Compassionate, gracious, and slow to anger
questions.explanation: Verse 8 names compassion, grace, patience, and abundant loving devotion. These qualities shape the psalm’s praise.

questions.prompt: What does the psalm say God remembers about people?
options: That they can carry every burden alone
questions.explanation: God knows our frame and remembers that we are dust. The verse places human limits within the picture of His fatherly compassion.

days.progression: Prayer now moves into daily choices. James connects asking God for wisdom with patient listening and action.
days.reflection: Where do you need wisdom—and what faithful action is already clear?
days.prayerPrompt: Ask God for wisdom in one decision, then name the faithful action you already know you can take.

questions.prompt: What does James say to do when we lack wisdom?
questions.explanation: James directs those who lack wisdom to ask God, who gives generously.

questions.prompt: What pattern does James urge in conversation?
options: Quick to listen, slow to speak, slow to anger
questions.explanation: James calls for patient listening and restraint in speech and anger.

questions.prompt: How should we respond to the word?
questions.explanation: James connects hearing with action. The word is meant to shape how we live.

days.progression: Yesterday’s invitation to ask for wisdom challenges self-sufficiency. Practice trust, faithfulness, and a willingness to be corrected.
days.reflection: Where would humility make a decision wiser, perhaps by listening, seeking counsel, or admitting a limit?
days.prayerPrompt: Name a choice before God and ask for a faithful heart that is willing to learn.

questions.prompt: Which two qualities does this passage say should not leave you?
questions.explanation: Verse 3 pictures loving devotion and faithfulness as something to wear and write on the heart. Wisdom is meant to shape character.

questions.prompt: What does the passage warn against leaning on?
options: The value of learning from others
questions.explanation: Verses 5–6 call for wholehearted trust in the LORD and acknowledgment of Him in all one’s ways. The contrast challenges self-reliance.

questions.prompt: What attitude toward the LORD’s discipline does the passage urge?
options: Treat every correction as proof of rejection
questions.explanation: Verses 11–12 connect the LORD’s discipline with love. In this passage, being willing to learn belongs with trusting Him.

days.theme: Words that make room for grace
days.progression: A teachable heart changes conversation. Notice how truth, useful speech, and kindness serve the people who hear you.
days.reflection: What conversation could be different if your aim were to build someone up while speaking truthfully?
days.prayerPrompt: Ask for truthful, helpful words and the tenderness to choose kindness in a difficult conversation.

questions.prompt: What reason does Paul give for speaking truthfully to a neighbor?
options: Honesty means every opinion must be shared
We are members of one another
questions.explanation: Paul links truthful speech to shared belonging. What one member says affects the others.

questions.prompt: What kind of speech does Paul encourage?
options: What builds up the person in need
questions.explanation: Verse 29 asks whether words build up the person in need and bring grace to listeners. The listener’s good matters.

questions.prompt: What pattern does Paul give for forgiving one another?
options: Keeping a record of every old wrong
questions.explanation: Paul joins kindness and tenderheartedness with forgiveness, pointing to how God forgave in Christ as the pattern.

days.progression: Yesterday’s helpful words are part of a larger pattern. Paul describes a life of loving service and Spirit-shaped character.
days.reflection: Which quality in the fruit of the Spirit could you practice in one ordinary situation today?
days.prayerPrompt: Ask the Spirit to grow patience, kindness, or self-control in a specific relationship or task.

questions.prompt: How does Paul tell believers to use their freedom?
options: Make their own desires the only guide
Prove they have no responsibilities to others
questions.explanation: Paul turns the discussion of freedom toward loving service. Freedom is not described as permission to disregard other people.

questions.prompt: Which group contains only qualities named as the fruit of the Spirit?
questions.explanation: Verses 22–23 list qualities including patience, kindness, and gentleness. They describe character rather than status or possessions.

questions.prompt: Because believers live by the Spirit, what does Paul urge them to do?
options: Walk in step with the Spirit
questions.explanation: Paul connects life by the Spirit with walking in step with the Spirit. The next verse warns against conceit, provocation, and envy.

days.progression: Wisdom reaches beyond private habits. Micah connects remembered deliverance with justice, mercy, and a humble walk with God.
days.reflection: Where can you act fairly, show mercy, and stay humble in a real decision today?
days.prayerPrompt: Ask God to help you recognize what is fair and merciful, and to take one humble action.

questions.prompt: What act does the LORD ask His people to remember?
options: Bringing them out of slavery in Egypt
Keeping them from ever needing guidance
questions.explanation: The LORD recalls bringing the people out of Egypt and redeeming them from slavery. His questions begin with remembered faithfulness.

questions.prompt: What question is being explored immediately before verse 8?
options: Which city has the strongest walls
Who will become the next king
What to bring when coming before the LORD
questions.explanation: Verses 6–7 ask about approaching the LORD with increasingly extravagant offerings. Verse 8 turns attention to the life God requires.

questions.prompt: Which three responses does Micah name as what the LORD requires?
options: Act justly, love mercy, and walk humbly with God
Gain influence, seek comfort, and avoid correction
Make a spectacle, win praise, and defend every choice
questions.explanation: Verse 8 brings justice, mercy, and humility together. The answer concerns how people live before God and with others.

days.progression: Justice and mercy become personal in the people nearby. Return to listening at Jesus’ feet, now alongside His call to practical compassion.
days.reflection: Who might need your attention and practical care today?
days.prayerPrompt: Bring to mind someone whose need you might overlook, and ask for attention, wisdom, and a practical way to care.

questions.prompt: Who shows mercy to the wounded man in Jesus’ parable?
questions.explanation: The Samaritan sees the wounded man and has compassion. He crosses a social boundary to give practical care.

questions.prompt: How does Jesus conclude the conversation about the neighbor?
questions.explanation: Jesus directs the expert in the law to imitate the mercy shown in the story.

questions.prompt: What is Mary doing when Martha asks Jesus to intervene?
questions.explanation: Mary sits at the Lord’s feet and listens to His message. Jesus defends her attention to Him.

days.progression: Practical mercy needs a patient heart. Paul measures impressive gifts and actions by the love that gives them meaning.
days.reflection: Where could patience or kindness change the way you offer help today?
days.prayerPrompt: Ask for love that is patient, truthful, and kind in a relationship you find easy to overlook.

questions.prompt: What does Paul compare impressive speech without love to?
options: A fruitful vine or well-watered garden
A lamp giving light to the house
A ringing gong or clanging cymbal
questions.explanation: The image of a gong or cymbal emphasizes noise without love. Paul begins by questioning the value of impressive expression on its own.

questions.prompt: Which description of love does Paul give here?
options: Eager to boast and keep rank
Quick to envy and insist on praise
questions.explanation: Verse 4 describes love through patience and kindness and says it does not envy, boast, or take pride.

questions.prompt: Of faith, hope, and love, which does Paul call the greatest?
questions.explanation: Paul says that faith, hope, and love remain, and that the greatest of these is love. This conclusion gathers the chapter’s emphasis.

days.theme: You have a place to give
days.progression: Patient love grows in a shared life. Paul pictures different gifts belonging to one body and calls for attention to others’ joys and sorrows.
days.reflection: What gift or capacity could you offer, and whose joy or sorrow could you make room for?
days.prayerPrompt: Thank God for someone whose gifts differ from yours, and ask how you can serve together.

questions.prompt: What picture does Paul use for the relationship among believers?
options: One body with many members and different functions
A contest with room for only one winner
Separate households with no responsibilities to each other
questions.explanation: Verses 4–5 compare believers to one body with different members. Difference and belonging are held together.

questions.prompt: What practical responses to others’ needs does Paul name?
questions.explanation: Paul calls for sharing with believers in need and practicing hospitality. Shared life takes a practical form.

questions.prompt: How does Paul say to respond to people who rejoice or weep?
options: Give everyone the same cheerful speech
Keep a distance from strong emotions
Rejoice with them and weep with them
questions.explanation: Verse 15 invites participation in others’ joy and grief. Love attends to the situation the other person is actually in.

days.progression: Belonging makes room for help when people struggle. Today joins gentleness, mutual burden-bearing, and perseverance in doing good.
days.reflection: Is there a burden you can help carry, or one you need to let a trustworthy person help you carry?
days.prayerPrompt: Ask for humility to receive help and gentleness to offer it, without comparing yourself with others.

questions.prompt: How should someone caught in a trespass be restored?
options: With no awareness of the helper’s own weakness
questions.explanation: Paul calls for gentle restoration and also tells the helper to watch themselves. Care and humility belong together.

questions.prompt: What does Paul ask believers to carry for one another?
options: Their reasons to avoid doing good
questions.explanation: Verse 2 directly calls for carrying one another’s burdens. It places mutual support alongside the personal responsibility described nearby.

questions.prompt: What does Paul urge when doing good becomes tiring?
options: Do not grow weary or give up
Care only when gratitude is guaranteed
Wait until helping requires no effort
questions.explanation: Verses 9–10 urge perseverance and doing good as opportunities arise. The instruction includes good toward everyone, with particular care for the family of faith.

days.progression: Mutual help becomes an ongoing practice. Gather the lessons of community into drawing near, holding hope, and encouraging one another.
days.reflection: Whom could you encourage toward love and a concrete good action this week?
days.prayerPrompt: Thank God for His faithfulness and ask how you can strengthen someone else’s hope today.

questions.prompt: How does the writer invite readers to draw near?
options: With a claim to be more important than others
With a need to hide every uncertainty from God
With a sincere heart and full assurance of faith
questions.explanation: Verse 22 invites sincere, confident approach to God. It follows the passage’s account of the access opened through Jesus.

questions.prompt: Why should readers hold firmly to the hope they profess?
options: The One who promised is faithful
Their circumstances are certain to remain easy
They have no further need for one another
questions.explanation: The reason given is the faithfulness of the One who promised. Hope rests on His character.

questions.prompt: What should readers consider how to encourage in one another?
questions.explanation: Verses 24–25 connect love and good deeds with meeting and encouraging one another. Community supports a practiced hope.

days.progression: Hope is needed when serving and waiting leave you tired. Return to the shepherd’s care from day one and receive the promise of renewed strength.
days.reflection: What does patient hope in God make possible for you today?
days.prayerPrompt: Tell God where you are tired, and ask for patient hope and strength for the next necessary step.

questions.prompt: What remains when grass withers and flowers fall?
questions.explanation: Isaiah contrasts fragile human life with the enduring word of God.

questions.prompt: How does Isaiah describe God’s care for His flock?
options: He gathers the lambs in His arms
He leaves them to find their way
questions.explanation: The passage pictures the LORD as a shepherd who gathers and gently leads His flock.

questions.prompt: Who will renew their strength?
options: Those who rely only on youth
Those who wait upon the LORD
questions.explanation: The promise concerns waiting upon the LORD. Isaiah has just said that even young people grow weary.

days.progression: Renewed strength does not mean trouble is imaginary. This psalm places God’s presence amid shaking earth and raging nations.
days.reflection: What feels unsettled, and what would it mean to seek God’s help within it rather than waiting for perfect calm?
days.prayerPrompt: Name what feels unstable and ask to remember God’s presence as you respond wisely to it.

questions.prompt: How does the psalm first describe God?
options: Our refuge and strength, a present help in trouble
A distant observer waiting for trouble to end
A reward only for those who never feel afraid
questions.explanation: The opening calls God a refuge, strength, and help in trouble. His help is described within trouble, not only after it.

questions.prompt: Which assurance is repeated in the psalm’s refrain?
options: No nation will ever rage again today
The LORD of Hosts is with us
People can secure themselves without help
questions.explanation: Verse 7 names God’s presence and calls the God of Jacob a fortress. The same assurance returns in verse 11.

questions.prompt: What does the psalm say God brings to an end throughout the earth?
questions.explanation: Verse 9 describes God making wars cease and breaking weapons. The following call to be still sits within this picture of His power among the nations.

days.theme: When hope has no easy words
days.progression: God’s help also reaches the times when relief is unseen and prayer is hard. Paul joins groaning, patience, and the Spirit’s help.
days.reflection: What are you waiting for, and how could you make room for both honest grief and patient hope?
days.prayerPrompt: Offer even a wordless concern to God, asking for the Spirit’s help in your weakness.

questions.prompt: How does Paul describe the present experience of the whole creation?
options: Already free from every form of decay
Groaning together in the pains of childbirth
Unconcerned with what will come next
questions.explanation: Paul describes creation as groaning, using the image of childbirth. The surrounding verses hold present suffering together with future hope.

questions.prompt: How does Paul say to wait for what is hoped for but not yet seen?
options: By insisting it is already visible
By denying that waiting is difficult
questions.explanation: Verse 25 names patience as the response to unseen hope. The passage has already acknowledged suffering and inward groaning.

questions.prompt: Who helps in weakness when believers do not know how to pray?
options: Only those who have perfect words
The approval of the surrounding crowd
questions.explanation: Verse 26 says the Spirit helps in weakness and intercedes when people do not know how to pray. Inadequate words do not place them beyond help.

days.progression: The journey’s hope comes into focus in the risen Jesus. Follow Mary from grief and confusion toward recognition and witness.
days.reflection: What do you notice about Mary’s movement from tears to telling others what she has seen?
days.prayerPrompt: Bring your grief and questions to Jesus, and ask for courage to share hope with gentleness.

questions.prompt: What does Mary Magdalene first notice when she reaches the tomb?
options: The entrance has been sealed with another stone
The disciples are already gathered inside
The stone has been removed from the entrance
questions.explanation: John begins the scene while it is still dark. Mary sees the removed stone before she understands what has happened.

questions.prompt: What does Jesus say just before Mary responds, “Rabboni”?
options: An instruction to return to Galilee
The names of all the disciples
questions.explanation: Jesus addresses Mary by name, and she responds by calling Him Teacher. The scene moves from nonrecognition to a personal encounter.

questions.prompt: What does Mary announce to the disciples?
options: There is no message to share
questions.explanation: Verse 18 records Mary’s announcement that she has seen the Lord and her report of what He said. Her encounter becomes a witness to others.

days.progression: Finish where the journey began, with God’s presence and care, now pictured in the promise of all things made new. Carry trust, prayer, wisdom, and love into the days ahead.
days.reflection: Which practice from these thirty days do you want to carry forward, and how does this picture of hope shape it?
days.prayerPrompt: Thank God for what you have noticed, name one practice to continue, and pray for those who are grieving or longing for renewal.

questions.prompt: What does the voice from the throne announce about God’s dwelling?
options: God will dwell with His people
God will remain forever out of reach
God’s people must build a path into heaven
questions.explanation: The announcement centers on God dwelling with people and being their God. The vision’s hope is deeply relational.

questions.prompt: What does this vision say God will do for people’s tears?
options: Require them to conceal every tear
Wipe every tear from their eyes
Leave tears outside the promise of renewal
questions.explanation: Verse 4 pictures God wiping away tears and the end of death, mourning, crying, and pain. It describes the promised new creation, not a claim that present suffering has already ended.

questions.prompt: What does the One seated on the throne declare?
options: Nothing that is broken can be renewed
Only the strongest may receive hope
questions.explanation: Verse 5 declares the making of all things new and calls the words faithful and true. This is the promise with which the sequence closes.

journeys.title: Rest for the weary
journeys.description: God’s care, an invitation, and a peace that stays.

sequence.title: A life rooted in grace
sequence.subtitle: Thirty connected days of Scripture, reflection, and prayer
sequence.summary: Begin with God’s care, learn the way of Jesus, bring your life into prayer, practice wisdom, grow in community, and carry hope into ordinary days.
sequence.readingGuide: Read the passage, explore three questions, pause with the reflection, and pray in your own words. Continue from where you left off; there is no need to rush.

progression.title: Receive God’s care
progression.description: Begin with care, grace, welcome, rest, and mercy. Receive before you try to achieve.

progression.title: Learn the way of Jesus
progression.description: Respond to grace by following Jesus, remaining close, listening, serving, and practicing His words.

progression.title: Bring your life into prayer
progression.description: Let following Jesus shape prayer: trust, honest lament, persistent asking, thanksgiving, and praise.

progression.title: Practice wisdom every day
progression.description: Carry prayer into decisions, speech, character, justice, and humble action.

progression.title: Grow in love together
progression.description: Practice wisdom with others through mercy, patient love, shared gifts, mutual help, and encouragement.

progression.title: Keep walking in hope
progression.description: Bring the whole journey into weariness, trouble, waiting, resurrection, and the promise of renewal.
